Buckfast
BUK-fast
n. (an abbey on the Dart in Devon, Benedictine from 1018, Cistercian from 1147, dissolved 1539, and rebuilt on its own medieval foundations between 1907 and 1938)
Old English bucca, a buck or stag, with fasten or faesten, a stronghold — the deer's stronghold on the river Dart.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Buckfast is the one English abbey whose church was raised twice. Founded about 1018, it became Savigniac and then Cistercian, was dissolved in 1539, and its stones were quarried for two centuries until nothing of the church stood above ground. In 1882 a community of French Benedictines expelled from their own country bought the site, uncovered the medieval foundations, and from 1907 built a new church on them — a handful of monks laying the stone themselves, never more than six at a time, finishing in 1938. Whatever a Reformed reader makes of the community, the act answers a text exactly. “And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12), and the title that follows is the point of the whole passage: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12). Nehemiah's word to a demoralised city has the same shape — “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17) — and the promise underneath both is God's own: “I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old” (Amo 9:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines restore as to return to a former state, to repair, to rebuild; and breach as the act of breaking, a gap, an opening made by breaking.

expand to see more

RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former owner. To bring back to a former good state; to repair; to rebuild.

BREACH, n. The act of breaking, or state of being broken; a rupture; a break; a gap; the space between the severed parts of a solid body parted by violence.

FOUNDATION, n. The basis or ground-work of any thing; that on which any thing stands, and by which it is supported.

WASTE, a. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; uncultivated.

ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.

Key Scripture

Isa 58:12 — "And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in."

Neh 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Amo 9:11 — "In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:"

Isa 61:4 — "And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations."

Modern Corruption

The one English abbey rebuilt on its own foundations, four centuries after it was pulled down.

expand to see more

The corruption near this entry is the sentimental reading of restoration — the idea that putting a building back is the same as recovering what it was for. Isaiah's promise is to a people, and the waste places are rebuilt by men whose fast God has accepted; the chapter spends its first half demolishing a religion of observance without mercy. A rebuilt church that does not “deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7) has repaired a wall and nothing else.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's restoring work runs through ordinary men laying actual stone, and that he takes the credit for it. “will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen” (Amo 9:11) is quoted by James at the Jerusalem council and applied to the ingathering of the Gentiles — the rebuilding that matters is of a people, and buildings are at best its sign.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English bucca faesten, the buck's stronghold; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; Hebrew perets (H6556), a breach; Hebrew qum (H6965), to raise up; Hebrew chorbah (H2723), a waste or ruin.

expand to see more

Old English bucca + faesten — the stronghold by the deer ford.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17).

Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach, a gap; “The repairer of the breach” (Isa 58:12).

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to raise up; “and I will raise up his ruins” (Amo 9:11).

Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste place, a ruin; “And they shall build the old wastes” (Isa 61:4).

Usage

"“thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12) — literally true at Buckfast."

"“they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4) — the prophet's word for a quarried site."

"“that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17) — the motive that is not vanity."
